note_claims.claim: The patient is presenting with fever and right earache.
The patient has had a fever since Tuesday evening (2 days), with a maximum recorded temperature of 38.9 °C at home.
The patient has been pulling at the right ear and was unsettled overnight.
The patient has reduced her appetite but is drinking well, and is passing urine normally.
The patient has vomited once on Tuesday and has not vomited since.
The patient has had a runny nose for about a week preceding the current symptoms.
The patient has no rash.
The patient's brother had chickenpox two weeks ago, and the patient has not had chickenpox.
The patient is alert and playing this morning.
The patient has no breathing difficulty.
The patient is previously well and her immunisations are up to date.
The patient has been given paracetamol intermittently.
The patient has no regular medications and no known drug allergies.
The patient's vital signs are Temperature 38.4 °C, Heart Rate 130, and Breathing Rate 26.
The patient's hands and feet are warm, and the capillary refill is under two seconds.
The left tympanic membrane is normal, and the right tympanic membrane is red and bulging.
The patient's throat is mildly erythematous.
The patient's neck is supple with no meningism.
The patient's chest is clear, and there is no rash on her skin.
The impression is Right acute otitis media.
There are no features of serious bacterial illness.
There is a recent chickenpox contact.
The plan includes regular analgesia with paracetamol 180 mg (7.5 mL of 120 mg/5 mL) up to four times daily and ibuprofen 100 mg (5 mL of 100 mg/5 mL) three times daily with food.
A back-up prescription for amoxicillin 250 mg three times daily for 5 days is planned, to start today.
A leaflet on chickenpox is given.
Safety-netting includes contacting the GP or 111 if the fever lasts more than 5 days in total, if there is ear discharge, or if the patient is not improving after 3 days.
Safety-netting includes reporting if the patient develops chickenpox and seems very unwell.

transcript_facts.fact: The patient has had a temperature and keeps pulling at her ear.
The duration of the fever was corrected from two days to three days (Monday evening).
The temperature measured last night was 38.9 °C.
The patient has been pulling at the right ear, mostly.
The patient reports that her ear hurts.
The patient is not eating much but is drinking okay (juice and milk).
The patient is in pants during the day but is still weeing normally, a few times today already.
The patient was sick once on Tuesday but has not since, and has no diarrhoea.
The patient has had a runny nose for about a week before all this started.
The patient has no rash, and her brother had chickenpox two weeks ago.
The patient has never had chickenpox.
The patient is grumpy but herself and was playing with her brother this morning.
The patient reports no problems breathing.
The patient is healthy and all her vaccinations are done.
The patient takes no regular medicines and has no allergies.
The patient has been given Calpol only when she seems really bad.
Examination findings include Temperature 38.4 °C, Heart Rate 130, Breathing Rate 26, warm hands and feet, and capillary refill under two seconds.
Examination findings include the left eardrum is normal, the right eardrum is red and bulging, and the throat is a little red.
Examination findings include the chest being clear and no rash on the skin.
The clinician suggests the finding looks like a middle ear infection on the right side.
The clinician suggests giving paracetamol 180 milligrams (7.5 mL of 120 mg/5 mL) up to four times a day and ibuprofen 100 milligrams (5 mL of 100 mg/5 mL) three times a day with food.
The clinician plans to provide a back-up prescription for amoxicillin 250 milligrams three times a day for 5 days.

Urgent signs for calling 999 or going to A&E include a rash that doesn't fade when pressed with a glass, becoming very drowsy or hard to wake, struggling to breathe, or stopping drinking and not weeing.
Urgent signs for contacting the GP or 111 include fever lasting more than five days in total, noticing any discharge from the ear, or not improving after three days.
The clinician advises that the patient may get chickenpox in the next week or so since she has been exposed, and to let them know if she seems very unwell with it.

findings.transcript_evidence: Since Tuesday night, so two days. No, hang on, it was Monday. It was the night of her swimming lesson, so Monday evening. Three days.
findings.rationale: The note incorrectly states the duration of the fever as 2 days, whereas the transcript corrects this to 3 days (Monday evening).
